clinicalPearls: A distal myopathy typically presenting in young adulthood with weakness of the posterior calf, so that patients notice difficulty standing on tiptoe or running
Wasting begins in the gastrocnemius and soleus, in contrast to the anterior distal weakness of several other distal myopathies
Caused by mutations in DYSF encoding dysferlin, and inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, part of the dysferlinopathy spectrum that also includes limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
Serum creatine kinase is characteristically very high, often markedly so, which is a useful pointer
Weakness spreads over time to involve the thighs and upper limbs, and the same DYSF mutations can produce a proximal limb-girdle phenotype even within one family
Muscle biopsy shows dystrophic changes with reduced or absent dysferlin on immunostaining, sometimes with an inflammatory infiltrate that can mimic myositis
Immunosuppression is ineffective, so distinguishing it from inflammatory myopathy avoids inappropriate treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Miyoshi myopathy is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in DYSF, the gene encoding dysferlin, a membrane protein concentrated at the sarcolemma that is essential for the calcium-dependent resealing of the muscle-fibre membrane after injury. When dysferlin is deficient, small membrane disruptions that occur with normal muscle activity are not repaired efficiently, leading to progressive membrane damage, leakage of muscle enzymes and fibre degeneration. The resulting dystrophic process preferentially begins in the posterior lower-leg muscles in the Miyoshi phenotype, and impaired membrane repair may also provoke a secondary inflammatory response that can be mistaken histologically for an inflammatory myopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (including other dysferlinopathy phenotypes)
Other distal myopathies such as GNE and tibial (anterior) distal myopathies
Metabolic myopathies causing exercise intolerance and high creatine kinase
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase, characteristically markedly elevated
Muscle magnetic resonance imaging demonstrating posterior calf and later thigh involvement
Muscle biopsy with dysferlin immunostaining and evaluation of monocyte dysferlin expression
Assessment to exclude an inflammatory myopathy when the biopsy shows inflammation
redFlags: Being started on immunosuppression for a presumed inflammatory myopathy
Rapidly progressive proximal weakness suggesting a limb-girdle phenotype
Loss of ambulation requiring rehabilitation input
reference.prognosis: Miyoshi myopathy is slowly progressive, with weakness spreading from the calves to more proximal muscles over years to decades; many patients eventually need walking aids, but respiratory and cardiac involvement are relatively uncommon and lifespan is often near normal.
pitfalls: Mistaking the inflammatory biopsy findings for polymyositis and giving ineffective immunosuppression
Overlooking the very high creatine kinase as a clue to a dysferlinopathy
Assuming a purely distal disorder, when proximal limb-girdle phenotypes share the same gene
Attributing early calf weakness to a neuropathy rather than a myopathy
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Recognise there is no disease-modifying drug and base care on physiotherapy with a graded exercise and stretching programme to preserve function and prevent contractures
Avoid corticosteroids, which do not help dysferlinopathy and may worsen it despite biopsy inflammation mimicking myositis
Provide mobility aids, orthoses and occupational therapy as distal then proximal weakness progresses
Undertake periodic respiratory and cardiac assessment, although these are relatively uncommon in this phenotype
Support weight and metabolic health to reduce load on weakening muscle
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive DYSF inheritance and test at-risk relatives
Refer to a specialist neuromuscular service for multidisciplinary care and access to dysferlinopathy trials
